lesson.title: Trig Identities: The Algebra Rules of the Unit Circle
lesson.summary: Trigonometric identities are equations that hold true for every angle, turning the geometry of the unit circle into an algebraic toolkit you will lean on constantly once calculus starts differentiating and integrating trig functions.
lesson.body:
A trigonometric identity is an equation involving sine, cosine, tangent, or their relatives that is true for every angle where both sides are defined, not just for one special angle. That "true for every angle" part is what makes identities useful: once you know one holds everywhere, you can substitute it into a messier expression to simplify it, without checking each case individually. This turns the unit circle, which is fundamentally a picture, into an algebraic toolkit you can manipulate with the same rules you use for polynomials and fractions.

Recall that the unit circle places a point (cos theta, sin theta) at angle theta measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis, and that every point on the circle satisfies x^2 + y^2 = 1 because the radius is 1. Substituting x = cos theta and y = sin theta immediately gives the most important identity in trigonometry: cos^2 theta + sin^2 theta = 1, called the Pythagorean identity because it is really just the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit circle's radius. Dividing that equation by cos^2 theta or sin^2 theta produces two companion identities, 1 + tan^2 theta = sec^2 theta and 1 + cot^2 theta = csc^2 theta, which you will lean on when integrating expressions containing tan^2 x or sec x.

A second family, the angle-sum and double-angle identities, describes how trig functions behave when angles combine. The most common are sin(2 theta) = 2 sin theta cos theta and cos(2 theta) = cos^2 theta minus sin^2 theta. These are not new facts pulled from nowhere; they follow from the angle-sum formulas sin(a+b) = sin a cos b + cos a sin b and cos(a+b) = cos a cos b minus sin a sin b, simply with a = b = theta.

Two more families are worth knowing early. The reciprocal identities simply restate a function in terms of its flipped partner: csc theta = 1/sin theta, sec theta = 1/cos theta, and cot theta = 1/tan theta. The power-reduction identities go the other way, trading a squared trig function for a sum involving a double angle, such as sin^2 theta = (1 - cos(2 theta))/2 and cos^2 theta = (1 + cos(2 theta))/2, both of which follow directly from rearranging cos(2 theta) = 1 - 2 sin^2 theta = 2 cos^2 theta - 1. This particular pair becomes indispensable once you start integrating, because there is no simple antiderivative rule for a squared sine or cosine sitting by itself, but there is a very simple one once it has been rewritten as a sum involving cos(2x).

Let's check the double-angle identity at a concrete angle, to make sure it actually holds rather than just being a symbolic claim. Take theta = pi/6, which is 30 degrees. From the unit circle, sin(pi/6) = 1/2 and cos(pi/6) = sqrt(3)/2. The right side of the identity gives 2 sin(pi/6) cos(pi/6) = 2 times (1/2) times (sqrt(3)/2) = sqrt(3)/2. Now check the left side directly: 2 theta = pi/3, which is 60 degrees, and sin(pi/3) = sqrt(3)/2. Both sides equal sqrt(3)/2, so the identity checks out at this angle, exactly as it must at every angle where it is defined.

Identities become essential once you start doing calculus with trig functions, because raw expressions like sin^2 x or sin x cos x are often awkward to differentiate or integrate directly, while an identity can rewrite them into a friendlier form first. Simplifying before you differentiate, rather than after, is a habit worth building now, and it depends entirely on having a reliable stock of identities you trust because you have verified them, not because you memorized them without checking.
